Realized trading losses, Day 46 (2026-08-05).

8 accounts hit their $2,000 max drawdown that session (the funded account, the two evaluations close to passing, and additional evaluation accounts blown during the tilt spree) — 8 x $2,000 = $16,000.

This is separate from the ~$800 spent re-purchasing/resetting evaluation account slots afterward (logged as its own entry the same day) — that's account-purchase fees, not trading losses. Total real cost of the day: ~$16,800.

Day 46 — Grade: F (tilt day)

Result: Blew 1 Funded Account & 2 Evaluation Accounts | ~$800 Lost in Evaluation Fees

Today was a tilt day.
I've already written about days like this before, and honestly, that's what frustrates me the most.
It's the same lesson coming back again.

I started the day with one funded account and two evaluation accounts, both evaluations being very close to passing.
That should have been enough.
The only thing I had to do was stay patient, follow my plan, and protect what I'd already built.
Instead, I did the exact opposite.

Coming into the session, my original idea was to look for shorts. That was my plan.
Then price didn't move the way I expected. Instead of staying patient and letting the market either confirm or invalidate my idea, I started changing my bias.
I bought. I sold. I bought again. I sold again.
At that point, I wasn't trading anymore. I was simply reacting to every move the market made. I completely lost control.

I blew the funded account. I blew both evaluations that were close to passing.
Instead of stopping there, I bought another five evaluation accounts. I even reset some of them after blowing them.
By the end of the session, I had spent roughly $800.
Right now, I only have two 50K evaluation accounts left. Everything else is gone.

Reflection
The frustrating part is that my original idea wasn't necessarily wrong. I wanted to short.
Instead of sticking with that idea until it was actually invalidated, I abandoned it because price wasn't moving the way I expected.
From there, I completely lost my process.
This wasn't a strategy problem. It wasn't a market problem. It was entirely psychological.
I've written many times that I need to learn to accept being wrong. Today proved that I still haven't solved that problem.
The first losing trade wasn't what ruined the day. My inability to stop after it did.
Every trade afterward became an attempt to fix the previous one. That's not trading. That's gambling.

Lessons
The biggest lesson today is one I've already written down before.
I need to stick with my original idea until the market genuinely invalidates it.
Not because I'm impatient. Not because price takes longer than expected. Only because the reason for the trade no longer exists.
I also need to recognize tilt much earlier. The moment I catch myself buying and selling without a clear reason, the trading day has to end. Immediately. No exceptions.
Another lesson is that I completely lost sight of the value of the accounts I already had.
One funded account and two evaluations that were close to passing were worth far more than chasing another trade.
I didn't protect that progress. I threw it away.

Final Thoughts
I'm not writing this because I'm happy about it. I'm writing it because I want an honest record of what happened.
Days like this aren't caused by a lack of market knowledge. They're caused by a lack of discipline.
The encouraging part is that I already know what needs to change. I've proven over the last few months that my process works when I actually follow it.
The problem isn't my strategy. The problem is that, every now and then, I stop trusting it.
Tomorrow isn't about making the money back. Tomorrow is about proving that I can follow my rules again. That's the only thing that matters.

Sticking to 1 trade a day til they are passed. Enough is enough...
